definition: Proactive means acting in advance to prevent problems rather than reacting to them.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word proactive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know proactive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rather than wait for breakdowns, the proactive fleet manager replaced every bus's brake pads on a fixed schedule, and roadside emergencies all but vanished.
Prepared means ready if trouble comes; proactive goes further - going out to meet trouble early and heading it off.
Preemptive outruns proactive: the proactive manager fixes weaknesses before problems grow, while a preemptive move strikes first to stop a specific threat from ever acting.

Forward-thinking praises the standing habit of planning with the future in mind — pension funds, ten-year roadmaps, tomorrow's skills taught today. Proactive is narrower and more urgent: acting now, in advance, so that specific problems never get the chance to happen. A forward-thinking board sketches where things are headed; a proactive one has already patched next month's weak spot.

Anticipatory means acting in expectation of something already on its way — the umbrella packed before the forecast rain. Proactive goes a step further: it means moving early on purpose to prevent problems, not merely to be ready when they land. Anticipatory braces for what is coming; proactive works so it never comes.

Proactive means acting in advance to prevent problems rather than reacting to them.
The orchard's new manager was proactive about frost: alarms that woke her when temperatures dipped, smudge pots fueled from September, the wind-machine crew booked in advance.
The freeze that ruined neighboring farms cost her a single row of trees.
Proactive describes acting before trouble arrives - spotting what could go wrong and moving first.
Its opposite is waiting for the problem and then scrambling; the proactive person has already scrambled, quietly, months earlier.
Proactive is the workplace word for heading trouble off early; it praises timing, not boldness.
Entrepreneurial, its unit-mate, is initiative aimed at building new ventures; proactive is initiative aimed at preventing problems.
And if the sentence is about striking first against one specific threat, the ladder's stronger rung, preemptive, is the sharper choice.

Nurse Delgado read the district's September memo about last winter's flu closures and decided her school would not repeat them.
Before a single student sneezed, she had soap dispensers mounted in every hallway and a vaccination clinic booked for the first week of October.
Colleagues teased her for fighting an enemy that had not shown up; she answered that the whole point was to make sure it never did.
Her proactive campaign looked almost boring by January: while two neighboring schools closed for a week apiece, hers recorded an ordinary month of sniffles.
The district later copied the plan, memo for memo, clinic for clinic.
